925.title: Forgiving the gunman (1983)
925.hook: John Paul II visits in prison the man who shot him
925.howItsDone: Catholics who volunteer in prison ministry visit inmates, often bringing Communion and listening, and some point to John Paul II's visit to Ağca and to Jesus's words in Matthew 25 as their pattern.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solidarity: a shipyard gate, a round table, and a country changed. Your line was without violence. Which worker did you thank? Today, the pope meets violence face to face. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

Cameras catch the scene, but not the words. Two chairs pulled close in a small prison cell in Rome. One man in white, one in a prisoner's clothes. They lean in until their heads nearly touch, and they talk quietly for a long time. At one point the man in white holds the other man's hand. The prisoner is Mehmet Ali Ağca. Some time before, in Saint Peter's Square, in front of a crowd, he raised a pistol and shot the man now sitting beside him. The visitor is John Paul the Second.
screen: `A CELL IN ROME, TWO CHAIRS.` → `THEY TALK FOR A LONG TIME.` → `THE GUNMAN AND THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Four moments make this story. First, the square. John Paul was riding slowly through the crowd in an open car when shots rang out. He was badly wounded and rushed to a hospital, and for a time it was not clear he would live. The gunman was caught on the spot. Second, the hospital. Within days, still weak, the pope spoke to the world by radio from his bed. He asked people to pray for the brother who had shot him, and said that he had sincerely forgiven him. Not the gunman. The brother. Third, the cell. Later, after his recovery, he went to the prison himself. He did not send a letter or a bishop. He went to the cell, sat down, and talked with the man. Afterward he said that what they talked about would remain a secret between them, and that he had spoken to him as a brother whom he had pardoned and who had his complete trust. Jesus, in Matthew's Gospel, names prison visits among the things done for him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." Fourth, what forgiveness did not do. Ağca stayed in prison for years after the visit. The pope did not pretend the shooting was small or that justice didn't matter. Catholic teaching holds forgiveness and justice side by side: you can release a debt in your heart and still let the courts do their work. Two chairs, two men, a held hand. What was said in that cell, they kept between them.
screen: `SHOTS IN SAINT PETER'S SQUARE.` · `FROM A HOSPITAL BED: MY BROTHER.` · `HE WENT TO THE CELL.` · `FORGIVENESS AND JUSTICE, BOTH.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse forgiving someone face to face. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something you can hold today. Picture two chairs, close. Picture them in the other one. You don't have to say it's fine. You can name what happened, and then, if you're ready, say: I forgive you. If you're not ready, notice that, and leave the chair there for another day. Forgiving never means putting yourself in harm's way. If you pray, you can pray for them, as the pope did, by name. The bell holds the time.
Forgiving the gunman. John Paul the Second, shot in Saint Peter's Square, forgave Mehmet Ali Ağca and went to visit him in prison.

Your line: he went to the cell. Today, if it's safe and you're ready, take one step toward the person in the other chair: a message, a call, or just their name in a prayer. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

926.title: Assisi, 1986
926.hook: leaders of many religions gather in Francis's town to pray for peace, each in their own way
926.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses and the Sant'Egidio community hold interreligious prayers for peace in the spirit of Assisi, where each tradition prays in its own way and the others listen in respectful silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving the gunman: two chairs in a Roman prison. Your line was he went to the cell. Did you take a step toward the other chair? Today, the same pope, and a very different gathering. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

Saffron, black, white, red: robes of every color fill the streets of a hill town in Italy, the town of Saint Francis. A Buddhist monk walks near an Orthodox bishop. Rabbis, Muslim leaders, Hindu teachers, Sikhs, Anglican and Lutheran church leaders, and leaders of traditional African and Native American religions have all come, because the pope invited them. They have come to pray for peace. But they will not say one prayer together. Each group goes off to its own place, to pray in its own way. Then they come back to one square and stand side by side. This is Assisi.
screen: `A HILL TOWN FULL OF ROBES.` → `INVITED BY THE POPE.` → `TO PRAY FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: John Paul the Second called it a World Day of Prayer for Peace. Here is how it worked, in four steps. First, the invitation. He asked the leaders of the world's religions to come to Assisi, the town of Francis, a saint remembered for peace and for meeting a sultan in a time of war. He asked them to fast and to pray, and he asked nobody to give up anything they believed. Second, apart. Each tradition went to its own church, hall or open space in the town and prayed in its own words and its own way. Catholics did not lead the others' prayers; nobody was asked to join anyone else's worship. Third, together. In the afternoon they gathered in front of the basilica of Saint Francis. One tradition after another offered its prayer for peace aloud, while everyone else stood and listened in silence. The pope put it this way: they were not going to pray together, but they were together in order to pray. Fourth, the worry and the answer. Some Catholics were uneasy, afraid it would look as if all religions were being blended into one. The pope answered that this was exactly what was not happening: each prayed as itself, with respect, and none pretended the differences away. Later popes have gone back to Assisi in the same spirit. Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." At Assisi, peacemaking began with something modest. Standing still while your neighbor prays.
screen: `AN INVITATION TO FAST AND PRAY.` · `APART: EACH PRAYS IN ITS OWN WAY.` · `TOGETHER: STANDING IN SILENCE.` · `NOT BLENDED, NOT PRETENDING.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold your neighbors of other faiths in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring up the people you know, or live near, who pray differently, or not at all: a coworker who fasts in a different season, a family down the street with a different holy day, a friend who keeps no tradition. Picture them standing in that square in Assisi, praying their own way while you stand quietly beside them. If you pray, you can pray for peace between religions in your own words, or with the line about peacemakers. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Assisi. The town of Saint Francis, where John Paul the Second invited leaders of the world's religions to pray for peace, each in their own way, side by side.
Your line: together, not blended. Today, ask one person of another faith, or none, what peace means in their tradition, and just listen. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

927.title: World Youth Day
927.hook: a gathering of young Catholics, begun by John Paul II, where a pope meets the young of the world
927.howItsDone: Catholic parishes and dioceses send groups of young people to World Youth Day, often raising money together for the trip, and those who stay home sometimes gather locally on the same days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Assisi: leaders of many religions praying for peace, side by side, each in their own words. Your line was together, not blended. Whose way of praying did you leave whole? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

A plain wooden cross is moving through an airport. Not a crucifix, just two beams, taller than the teenagers carrying it. They tip it to get it through the door, laughing, and a security guard holds the door open. The cross is on its way to a city where, in a few months, young Catholics from across the world will arrive with backpacks and flags, sleep on gym floors and in strangers' spare rooms, queue for hours in the sun, and sing in languages they don't speak. At the end they walk out to a field, spend the night under the open sky, and in the morning a pope says Mass for them. The gathering is called World Youth Day, though it lasts most of a week.
screen: `A WOODEN CROSS AT THE AIRPORT.` → `BACKPACKS, FLAGS, GYM FLOORS.` → `A NIGHT IN A FIELD.`

segments.voice: It started with an invitation. John Paul the Second, the pope you met a few days ago with be not afraid, invited the young to Rome, and then kept inviting them, in a different city each time. Later popes kept the invitation going. It became a habit of the Church: every few years, the young gather. Second, the cross. John Paul gave a simple wooden cross to the young people and asked them to carry it around the world. It travels from country to country before each gathering, and it's carried through prisons, hospitals, schools and parishes on the way. Beside it travels an icon of Mary. Third, the shape of the week. There's teaching from bishops in many languages, there's confession in tents and on folding chairs, there's music late into the night. Then comes the pilgrimage on foot to a big field, a night vigil with candles, and the closing Mass in the morning. The sleeping on the ground is part of it. Fourth, why the young. The prophet Joel promised a day when God's spirit would be poured out on everyone, and the Douay-Rheims gives his line: "your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions." And Paul writes to Timothy, a young church leader: "Let no man despise thy youth." The point is not that the young are the future of the Church, someday. In these texts they are part of it now, with visions of their own. Some come back changed. Some come back sunburned and tired and not sure what happened. The Church sends the invitation either way.
screen: `BEGUN BY JOHN PAUL II.` · `A WOODEN CROSS THAT TRAVELS.` · `TEACHING, CONFESSION, A NIGHT IN A FIELD.` · `THE YOUNG ARE PART OF IT NOW.` · then, large: `LET NO MAN DESPISE THY YOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for young Catholics, or simply hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one young person you actually know. A niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, the teenager who bags your groceries. Picture them with a backpack on, somewhere far from home, a little lost, a little excited. What would you want for them? If you pray, you can pray for them by name, maybe with Paul's line, let no man despise thy youth. If you don't, just hold them there and wish them good company. The bell holds the time.
World Youth Day. A gathering of young Catholics with the pope, begun by John Paul the Second, held in a different city each time, ending with a night in a field and a morning Mass.
Your line: the young gather. Today, take one young person seriously. Ask what they think about something that matters, and listen to the whole answer. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: The Day of Pardon (2000)
928.hook: in St Peter's, the pope publicly asks forgiveness for sins committed by Catholics through history
928.howItsDone: Catholics confess their own sins in the sacrament of penance and say the Confiteor, with its words through my fault, at the start of Mass; the Day of Pardon brought that language to the Church's own history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, World Youth Day: a wooden cross on the move, a night in a field. Your line was the young gather. Who did you listen to all the way through? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

On a Sunday in Lent, in St Peter's Basilica, a crucifix stands near an old pope. One after another, cardinals and bishops step forward. Each names a kind of wrong. Not wrongs done to the Church. Wrongs done by its own members. After each one there's silence, and then the pope speaks a prayer asking pardon, and the people answer. Before it ends, the pope goes to the crucifix and kisses it. He was John Paul the Second, frail by then. The Church remembers it as the Day of Pardon. A very old institution, under its own famous dome, saying out loud: we did this.
screen: `A CRUCIFIX IN ST PETER'S.` → `WRONGS DONE BY ITS OWN MEMBERS.` → `WE DID THIS.`

segments.voice: The prayers came in a set order. First, what was named. The prayers asked forgiveness for sins committed in the service of truth, for divisions among Christians, for sins against the people of Israel, for wrongs against love, peace and the dignity of peoples and cultures, against women, against the poor and the unborn. They were broad on purpose. Some listeners wanted more names and details; some thought it went too far. Both reactions were real. Second, who was asking. The Church teaches that the Church itself is holy, and also that its members sin. So the prayers were spoken for the sins of her sons and daughters, the members, past and present. Theologians had spent time on exactly that distinction and wrote a document about it, called Memory and Reconciliation. Third, the scripture underneath. The first letter of John says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." A Church that says that to each person in confession was saying it about itself. Fourth, the other half. In his homily that day the pope paired two things: we forgive, and we ask forgiveness. Catholics have an old phrase for owning a wrong, from the Confiteor, one of the prayers that can open Mass: through my fault. On that day it was said by a whole Church, about its own history. What it did not do was settle everything. An apology spoken in Rome is a beginning. What comes after it is the hard part, and some of that story comes tomorrow.
screen: `SINS NAMED, ONE BY ONE.` · `A HOLY CHURCH, MEMBERS WHO SIN.` · `IF WE SAY WE HAVE NO SIN.` · `WE FORGIVE, AND WE ASK FORGIVENESS.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH IS NOT IN US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask forgiveness for your part. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that went wrong between you and someone else, where the blame is shared. Don't add up their part. Just find your own piece of it, small or large, and name it plainly to yourself, the way those bishops did: one sentence, no excuses. If you pray, you can bring it to God, perhaps with the old words, through my fault. If you don't, just hold it honestly, without punishing yourself. The bell holds the time.
The Day of Pardon. A Lenten Sunday in St Peter's when John Paul the Second asked forgiveness for wrongs done by Catholics through history.
Your line: we ask forgiveness. Today, if there's someone owed an apology for your part, say it in one sentence, with no but at the end. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: The abuse crisis
929.hook: clergy abuse and cover-ups hurt children; survivors come first
929.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses commonly have safeguarding offices and require background checks and training for clergy, staff and volunteers who work with children; some keep a day of prayer for survivors of abuse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Day of Pardon, when a pope asked forgiveness for the sins of Catholics through history. Your line was we ask forgiveness. Today is part of why asking is not the end of it. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

A note before we start. Today's lesson is about the abuse of children by clergy, and about leaders who covered it up. Nothing graphic is described. If this touches your own life, you can stop here, or come back to it another day, and it's worth reaching out to someone you trust or a local support line. For everyone else: this is part of the long story of the Church in our time, and leaving it out would be its own kind of cover-up. Children and vulnerable adults were harmed by priests and religious they had every reason to trust. And when some of them spoke, they were not believed, or they were paid to stay quiet, while abusers were moved to new places. Today's word is what the Church calls the work of making sure that never happens again.
screen: `A NOTE BEFORE WE START.` → `HARM, AND THEN A COVER-UP.` → `TODAY'S WORD: SAFEGUARDING.`

segments.voice: Four things, said carefully. First, the harm was double. There was the abuse itself, and then there was what came after: survivors who told the truth and were doubted, families pressured into silence, abusers sent somewhere new. Public reports and investigations described this pattern. Second, who broke it open. Not, first of all, the Church's leaders. Survivors, who kept telling their stories, often for years; journalists and investigators who listened; and lay people and some clergy who refused to look away. Third, what the Church's leaders have said. Pope Francis wrote a letter to the whole Church in which he admitted that the Church had not acted in time, and he quoted Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it." Catholics also hear a hard warning from Jesus, that for anyone who leads one of these little ones astray, it would be better to be drowned in the sea with a millstone around the neck. Fourth, the word. Safeguarding means the plain, unglamorous rules that protect children and vulnerable adults now: background checks, training, never one adult alone with a child, clear ways to report, and reporting to civil authorities. Some dioceses and parishes now have a named safeguarding office. Survivors and their advocates say rules alone are not enough without honesty and accountability, and that work is not finished. Through all of it, one principle: survivors first. Not the reputation of an institution. Not the comfort of the people in charge. The people who were harmed.
screen: `THE ABUSE, AND THEN THE COVER-UP.` · `SURVIVORS BROKE THE SILENCE.` · `IF ONE MEMBER SUFFER.` · `SAFEGUARDING: RULES THAT PROTECT.` · then, large: `SURVIVORS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold survivors at the center, and if you want, support safeguarding. Settle, and breathe. You don't need to picture anything. Just bring to mind the people, often unnamed, who were harmed as children and then not believed. Let them be the first thing you think of, not the last. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for their healing, in whatever words you have. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with respect. And if you belong to a parish, you can find out later who its safeguarding contact is. The bell holds the time.
Safeguarding. The work of protecting children and vulnerable adults: training, checks, clear reporting, and putting survivors first.
Your line: survivors first. Today, if you're part of any group that has children in it, a parish, a team, a school, learn how someone would report a concern there. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

930.title: The Catechism (1992)
930.hook: a single summary of Catholic belief, written for the whole world
930.howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference in parish classes, adult formation and preparation for the sacraments, often citing it by paragraph number; shorter local catechisms and the Compendium draw on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard day: the abuse crisis, and the word safeguarding. Your line was survivors first. Did you find out how a concern would be reported where you belong? Day nine hundred thirty.

If someone asked you, what do Catholics actually believe, where would you send them? A priest, maybe. A website. A grandmother. For a long time the answer depended on where you lived: each country, sometimes each diocese, had its own little question-and-answer book. Children memorized them. Who made us? God made us. There had been a catechism for the whole Church once before, written after the Council of Trent for parish priests. Then the bishops of the world, meeting in Rome, asked for a new one: one book, for the whole Church, that set out the faith in order. It took years of drafting, and the bishops were asked for their comments. The result is a thick book with numbered paragraphs, sitting today on parish shelves and on phones. It's called the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
screen: `WHAT DO CATHOLICS BELIEVE?` → `A LITTLE BOOK FOR EACH PLACE.` → `ONE BOOK FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Open the book and its plan is plain. First, the shape. The Catechism is built in four parts, and once you know them the whole book opens up. The faith professed: the Creed, line by line. The faith celebrated: the liturgy and the sacraments. The faith lived: the life in Christ, including the Ten Commandments. And the faith prayed: prayer, ending with the Our Father, line by line. What Catholics believe, how they worship, how they live, and how they pray. Second, the numbers. Every paragraph has a number, and the book cross-references itself in the margins, so one paragraph about baptism points you to others about grace, about the Church, about water at Easter. People cite it by number, the way you'd cite a verse. Third, who it's for. John Paul the Second, in the document that introduced it, called it a sure norm for teaching the faith, meant first for bishops and teachers, and then for anyone who wants to know what the Church believes. It was never meant to replace local catechisms, but to be the reference they draw on. Fourth, the sources. Open it almost anywhere and the paragraphs are stitched from scripture, from the councils, from saints and early writers. Luke opens his Gospel by telling Theophilus why he wrote it, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." The Catechism sets out to do the same thing at the size of a whole Church: one summary, in order, so the faith can be known, not just guessed at.
screen: `FOUR PARTS: BELIEVE, WORSHIP, LIVE, PRAY.` · `NUMBERED PARAGRAPHS, CITED LIKE VERSES.` · `A SURE NORM FOR TEACHING.` · `STITCHED FROM SCRIPTURE AND SAINTS.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to read one paragraph. Settle, and breathe. Of the four parts, believe, worship, live, pray, which one are you most curious about right now? Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one with a question in it. Then name the question, in a few words, to yourself. What is grace? Why confession? What does the Church say about work? Hold that question gently, without trying to answer it yet. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. If you don't, just stay curious. The bell holds the time.
The Catechism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church: one summary of the faith, in four parts, in numbered paragraphs, for the whole Church.
Your line: one summary. Today, find the part of the Catechism that holds your question, and read one paragraph. Just one, slowly. Day nine hundred thirty.

931.title: Benedict XVI (2005–2013)
931.hook: a quiet theologian whose first encyclical was God is love
931.howItsDone: Catholics read the first letter of John at Mass at various points in the year, and parishes and charities sometimes study Deus caritas est for its teaching that care for the poor belongs to the Church's own life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Catechism: one book, four parts, numbered paragraphs. Your line was one summary. Which paragraph did you read? Today, a man who helped make that book, and then became pope. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

A new pope's first encyclical is watched closely. It's the first long letter he writes to the whole Church, and people read it for a program. This one came from a man who had spent his life as a professor and then as the Vatican's guardian of doctrine. Some expected rules. Its title, in Latin, was three words: Deus caritas est. God is love. It opens with a line from the first letter of John, and then it does something some readers did not expect from a strict theologian. It talks about eros, the love of desire, and about agape, the love that gives itself away, and it says the two belong together.
screen: `A FIRST LETTER, CLOSELY WATCHED.` → `SOME EXPECTED RULES.` → `DEUS CARITAS EST.`

segments.voice: His name was Joseph Ratzinger, and as pope he took the name Benedict. Four ways in. First, the scholar. He was a theologian before he was a bishop, a writer of books, more at home at a desk than on a balcony. He had worked on the Catechism you met yesterday, and for a long time he guarded Catholic teaching in Rome, which earned him critics as well as admirers. Second, the name. Benedict is the name of the monk of Nursia, whose rule shaped monasteries across Europe, and of Benedict the Fifteenth, a pope who pleaded for peace in a world war. Third, the letter. The first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, uses an older English word for love: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him." Charity there doesn't mean a donation. It's the Latin caritas, love itself. Benedict's letter starts there and then turns practical: if God is love, then the Church's care for the poor and the sick isn't a side activity. It belongs to what the Church is, as much as the sacraments and the preaching of the word. Fourth, what people disagree about. Some remember him as a brilliant, gentle teacher. Others remember the strict guardian of doctrine, or a papacy troubled by scandal. Both are part of the record. But when he wrote his first letter to the whole Church, he gave it a three-word title. And that brings the week to its end: from forgiving the gunman, through Assisi, World Youth Day, the Day of Pardon, the abuse crisis and the Catechism, to a pope whose first word to the Church was love.
screen: `JOSEPH RATZINGER, THE SCHOLAR.` · `THE NAME OF A MONK AND A PEACE POPE.` · `GOD IS CHARITY: LOVE ITSELF.` · `ADMIRED AND CRITICIZED.` · then, large: `GOD IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read 1 John 4, or begin with one verse of it. Settle, and breathe. Say the line slowly, in the old words: God is charity, and he that abideth in charity abideth in God. Then put a face on it. Who loved you when nothing was in it for them? A neighbor, a friend, a stranger who helped. Stay with that person for a while. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, simply be grateful. Later today, read the whole chapter; it's short. The bell holds the time.
Benedict the Sixteenth. Joseph Ratzinger, a theologian who became pope and whose first encyclical was Deus caritas est: God is love.
Your line: God is love. Today, do one act of charity in the old sense, love that costs you something, and don't mention it to anyone. Day nine hundred thirty-one.
